coverage_window.note: UK-focused run (Friday). A busier window than Thursday's, and the balance has shifted decisively from disclosure to exploitation: three of the ten entries are new campaigns with confirmed in-the-wild activity, two more are newly armed with public exploits, and two KEV deadlines expire today. Seven of ten entries are new. New and actively exploited: the hijacking of cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect administrative panels via a flaw in the third-party 'RMM+' extension family, pushing the 'SCKit' toolkit to 288 endpoints across 48 organisations inside 90 minutes from approximately 17:47 UTC on 11 November, with ConnectWise disabling five extensions across roughly 400 environments and at least six MSP consoles reported compromised (ranked first for its direct reach into the UK managed-service supply chain); Check Point Research's finding that PHP2Shell is being chained with CVE-2026-123039, a Gaia DynamicCLI privilege escalation, for root on Mobile Access gateways, then pivoted over SSH to VMware ESXi where the 'destroy_v6' wiper is executed - a destructive end state with no decryption path, in a second wave that went global from 2 November (ranked second); and the 'wfx-loot' campaign, in which 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts were used against 61,764 repositories to plant a CI credential stealer, with secrets already taken from at least 1,835 repositories, around 50 accounts holding package-publishing rights, and GitHub OIDC tokens exchanged for live AWS, Azure and GCP sessions - the industrialised form of the UK public-sector code exposure this feed has carried since 11 November (ranked third). Newly armed but not yet observed in use: 'Fortinet2Shell' (CVE-2026-121529, CVSS 9.1), a drive-by RCE as SYSTEM against FortiClient's loopback API now with public proof-of-concept code and most reliable where the FortiPAM agent is present; and 'SignDrop', a Windows CLFS local privilege escalation to SYSTEM published with a working PoC but no CVE, no advisory and no patch. Updated carry-overs: Apache CVE-2026-119618 now has a public reproduction lab and a Red Hat statement that a reliable exploit against a default HTTP/2 configuration has been demonstrated, though no sensor or honeypot telemetry showing real-world exploitation surfaced; CISA was reported on 12 November to have confirmed active exploitation of Outlook CVE-2026-124194, with Microsoft confirming NTLMv2 hash theft; and the Barracuda ESG chain plus Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 reach their KEV deadline TODAY, with the 9 November batch now overdue. UK corporate: two new leak-site listings in window (bristol-companies.com by Settra and sdcc.net, both 12 November), with Audio Note UK, A&O Shearman and Signworx carrying over and Maersk the only company-confirmed case. UK government: no new incident first reported inside this window was confirmed. The substantive UK government development is regulatory - the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill has returned to the Commons with managed service providers explicitly in scope as Relevant MSPs, which the ScreenConnect compromise at rank 1 illustrates with uncomfortable timing. Rotated out, all without in-window developments: the Turla 'Cereal' Exchange backdoor, the NCSC CyAS launch and the UK public-sector code exposure (both folded into ranks 10 and 3 respectively as context), SAP's November Patch Day, and Check Point's CopperDragon/Sparrow research.

vulnerabilities.title: ConnectWise ScreenConnect Cloud Consoles Hijacked Through 'RMM+' Third-Party Extension - 'SCKit' Toolkit Pushed to 288 Endpoints Across 48 Organisations in 90 Minutes; ConnectWise Disables Five Extensions Across ~400 Environments
affected_products: ConnectWise ScreenConnect - cloud-hosted instances (primary observed target)
ScreenConnect 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783 (both observed affected - running the latest release was not protective)
On-premises ScreenConnect deployments running any of the five 'RMM+' family extensions
Downstream: every endpoint managed by a compromised MSP's ScreenConnect instance
vulnerabilities.summary: UK corporate and UK public sector via managed service providers - the single most consequential new event in this window. Beginning at approximately 17:47 UTC on 11 November 2026, Huntress observed attackers taking control of cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect administrative panels and using them to push a bespoke toolkit tracked as 'SCKit' to at least 288 managed endpoints across 48 organisations. Every observed infection landed inside a 90-minute burst, which is the defining characteristic of this incident: the blast radius is not the remote-access tool, it is the downstream customer estate of whoever runs the console. The reported entry point is not a ScreenConnect product vulnerability but a flaw in 'RMM+', a third-party extension family for managing ScreenConnect sessions that uses a shared access key and thereby bypasses ScreenConnect's own authentication. ConnectWise has disabled five extensions in that family across roughly 400 ScreenConnect environments and states it has found no vulnerability in ScreenConnect itself and no compromise of its own infrastructure; its investigation into initial access is open. Reporting conflicts on whether the previously patched critical ScreenConnect flaw CVE-2026-84869 played any part - one outlet describes the campaign as exploitation of that now-patched flaw rather than a new vulnerability, while others state researchers have not established that it was successfully exploited here. Treat that CVE as disputed context, not as the confirmed vector. Post-access tradecraft is consistent across reports: the operators abused ScreenConnect's native 'Run command' function to execute as SYSTEM, added Microsoft Defender exclusions, installed a second rogue ScreenConnect client for redundant access, and staged further payloads. ConnectWise separately reported that the administrative consoles of at least six MSPs using cloud ScreenConnect were compromised; Morocco's DGSSI issued a national advisory and Sophos is investigating related unauthorised ScreenConnect deployments. UK relevance is direct and structural. ScreenConnect is a mainstay of the UK MSP and IT-support market, including providers serving local authorities, NHS primary-care and dental practices, schools and multi-academy trusts, and the SME supply chain into central government. This is the exact dependency the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill is being amended to regulate - see rank 10 - and it is the same shape as the attacks the NCSC's Annual Review flagged as driving UK incident volume. Both Huntress and ConnectWise warn administrators NOT to investigate a suspected infection by connecting to the host through ScreenConnect, because the technician's own machine can be taken in the process; use out-of-band access. Detail is from search-result summaries only; vendor pages were not retrievable from this environment.
recommended_actions: Today: ask every MSP and IT outsourcer with remote access to your estate, in writing, whether they run ConnectWise ScreenConnect, whether their instance is cloud-hosted, and whether any 'RMM+' family extension was installed. Treat a non-answer as a yes and isolate accordingly.

In on-premises ScreenConnect deployments, disable the RMM+ family extensions immediately - ConnectWise has already disabled them in ~400 cloud environments but on-premises operators must act themselves.

Do NOT triage a suspected infected endpoint over ScreenConnect. Use out-of-band access (EDR live response, direct console, separate RMM) - connecting through the compromised tool exposes the responder's workstation.

Hunt for the full set of ScreenConnect clients installed across your estate and reconcile against the authorised instance identifier; a second, unauthorised client is the campaign's persistence mechanism.

Hunt for Microsoft Defender exclusion additions created in the last 7 days, especially any created by a process parented to a ScreenConnect service - this preceded payload staging in the observed intrusions.
Hunt for any process executed as SYSTEM with a ScreenConnect service as the parent, concentrating on the 11 November 17:00-20:00 UTC window and the following 72 hours.
Rotate credentials, API keys and session tokens that any ScreenConnect-managed endpoint could reach, and force re-authentication for privileged accounts used by support technicians.
Obtain and ingest the Huntress and ConnectWise indicator lists directly - they were published with the research and are more current than any relayed summary.
Review and restrict ScreenConnect's 'Run command' capability by role; it is the execution primitive that turned console access into SYSTEM on 288 machines.

kql.name: Process executed by ScreenConnect service as SYSTEM (SCKit staging)
kql.description: Untested. Core detection: the operators used ScreenConnect's native Run command to execute as SYSTEM. Baseline your MSP's legitimate scripted activity first, then alert on anything outside it.
kql.query:
let SCProcs = dynamic(["screenconnect.clientservice.exe", "screenconnect.windowsclient.exe", "connectwisecontrol.clientservice.exe", "screenconnect.service.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (SCProcs)
| where AccountName in~ ("system", "nt authority\\system")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe", "regsvr32.exe", "msiexec.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Microsoft Defender exclusion added (SCKit pre-staging)
kql.description: Untested. Installation scripts added Defender exclusions before deploying payloads. Any exclusion added by a remote-management parent is high-signal; exclusions are rare and deliberate in most estates.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference", "ExclusionPath", "ExclusionProcess", "ExclusionExtension", "MpCmdRun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Exclusion", "DisableRealtimeMonitoring", "DisableIOAVProtection")
| extend ViaRemoteTool = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise"), "YES", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ViaRemoteTool, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by ViaRemoteTool desc, Timestamp desc

kql.name: Second / unauthorised ScreenConnect client installed
kql.description: Untested. The campaign installed a rogue ScreenConnect client alongside the legitimate one for redundant access. Replace the AuthorisedInstance string with your own instance identifier to make this precise.
kql.query:
let AuthorisedInstance = "REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-INSTANCE-ID";
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where FileName has_any ("ScreenConnect.Client", "ScreenConnect.WindowsClient", "ConnectWiseControl.Client", "ScreenConnect.ClientSetup")
   or FolderPath has_any ("ScreenConnect Client", "ConnectWise Control Client")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| extend Unexpected = iff(FolderPath has AuthorisedInstance, "expected", "REVIEW")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Unexpected, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Unexpected asc, Timestamp desc

kql.name: Burst detection - same command across many endpoints in a short window
kql.description: Untested. All observed infections occurred inside 90 minutes. This surfaces the pattern itself: one command line executing across an unusual number of distinct devices in a short period, which is how mass push via a hijacked console looks in telemetry.
kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise")
| summarize DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceName), Devices = make_set(DeviceName, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by ProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 90m)
| where DeviceCount >= 5
| extend SpreadMinutes = datetime_diff('minute', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| project Timestamp, DeviceCount, SpreadMinutes, FirstSeen, LastSeen, ProcessCommandLine, Devices
| order by DeviceCount desc

kql.name: ScreenConnect client beaconing to an unexpected relay
kql.description: Untested. A rogue client calls home to the attacker's relay, not yours. Add your legitimate relay FQDN(s) to the allowlist; everything else from a ScreenConnect process warrants investigation.
kql.query:
let KnownRelays = dynamic(["REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-RELAY.screenconnect.com", "REPLACE-WITH-YOUR-RELAY.hostedrmm.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("screenconnect", "connectwise")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl) or isnotempty(RemoteIP)
| extend Host = tolower(coalesce(RemoteUrl, RemoteIP))
| where not (Host has_any (KnownRelays))
| summarize Connections = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by Host, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemotePort
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.title: PHP2Shell Chained With Check Point Gaia DynamicCLI Privilege Escalation (CVE-2026-123039) for Root on Mobile Access Gateways, Then Pivot to VMware ESXi and 'destroy_v6' Wiper - Second Wave Now Global
affected_products: Check Point Security Gateways with the Mobile Access blade / Mobile Access portal enabled (initial access surface)
Check Point Gaia OS DynamicCLI interface (CVE-2026-123039, local privilege escalation to root, CVSS 7.8)
PHP-based web components vulnerable to PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
VMware ESXi hosts reachable over SSH from a compromised gateway (destructive stage)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - the most destructive confirmed exploitation in this window. Check Point Research published an investigation (covered 12-13 November by SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and others) showing that the PHP2Shell flaws are being chained with CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege escalation in the Gaia OS DynamicCLI interface rated CVSS 7.8, to obtain root on Check Point Security Gateways running the Mobile Access portal. This changes the character of the PHP2Shell story materially: it is no longer opportunistic webshell dropping, it is a full appliance takeover with a destructive end state. After rooting the gateway the operators deploy a backdoor tracked as TSGA, pivot over SSH to VMware ESXi hosts reachable from the gateway, and execute a Linux ELF wiper named 'destroy_v6' that recursively destroys the contents of a supplied directory, leaving politically themed ransom-style notes called DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt. This is destruction of the virtualisation layer, not encryption of it - there is nothing to decrypt and recovery depends entirely on offline backups. Two waves are described: a first wave from late October concentrated on Israeli organisations, and a broader follow-up wave from 2 November 2026 spanning multiple countries and sectors, including some of the same Israeli entities. Check Point states the escalation flaw was exploited against 'a couple of dozen customers'. Attribution is explicitly unsettled - Check Point says the evidence does not permit a high-confidence assessment of the operation's true nature, leaving open a genuine hacktivist-destructive campaign, an access-broker handoff, or a false flag; separately, Dream has linked PHP2Shell exploitation against Palo Alto firewalls to Chinese actors. UK relevance is immediate: Check Point gateways with Mobile Access are a common remote-access tier across UK local government, NHS trusts, legal and financial services and mid-market enterprise, and the pivot path gateway-to-ESXi mirrors precisely the pattern that caused prolonged outages in the UK retail and manufacturing incidents of the last eighteen months. Patches exist - reported fixed takes are R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132 and R81.20 Take 174 - but one vulnerability database entry still advises monitoring the vendor advisory, so confirm your exact take against Check Point directly. Critically, the PHP2Shell patches alone are not sufficient: exploitation began days before the 21 October fixes and escalated to mass exploitation shortly after, so any internet-facing Mobile Access portal unpatched between mid-October and now must be treated as potentially compromised and assessed, not merely updated.
recommended_actions: Identify every Check Point Security Gateway with the Mobile Access blade enabled and confirm its current take against Check Point's advisory; the reported fixed takes are R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132 and R81.20 Take 174.

Treat patching as insufficient on its own. Any Mobile Access portal exposed to the internet and unpatched between mid-October and the date you patched must be subjected to a compromise assessment, not just an upgrade.

vulnerabilities.title: 'wfx-loot' Campaign Abuses 4,837 Compromised GitHub Accounts to Plant a CI Credential Stealer Across 61,764 Repositories - Secrets Already Taken From 1,835+, ~50 Accounts Held Package-Publishing Rights
vulnerabilities.vendor: GitHub (platform abuse - not a GitHub product vulnerability)
affected_products: GitHub repositories with GitHub Actions workflows
GitHub Actions secrets and variables, GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC tokens and Actions runtime tokens
Cloud roles federated to GitHub OIDC in AWS, Azure and GCP
Package registries reachable from compromised accounts: npm, PyPI, Go, crates.io, Packagist
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - the window's clearest supply-chain risk, and the direct continuation of this feed's UK public-sector code-exposure thread. Aikido Security disclosed, with ThaiCERT reissuing it on 13 November, a campaign tracked as 'wfx-loot' in which 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts were used to target 61,764 repositories with a credential-stealing GitHub Actions payload. The operation began on 10 November 2026 with a reconnaissance step: pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes' opened from the hijacked accounts purely to test whether each account held write permission. Where it did, malicious commits followed - Helix reports 8,093 repositories received them - and the payload harvested GitHub Actions secrets and variables, the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, AI-service keys and developer-tool credentials. ThaiCERT states secrets were already stolen from at least 1,835 repositories; SecurityWeek puts the stealer's execution at over 1,800. The escalation that makes this critical rather than merely noisy is OIDC exchange: the payload trades GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure and GCP sessions, so a repository compromise becomes a live cloud-plane compromise without any long-lived cloud credential ever being stored in the repo. Roughly 50 of the compromised accounts also held rights to publish to npm, PyPI, Go, crates.io and Packagist, which is the mechanism by which this becomes a downstream problem for organisations that never used GitHub Actions at all. Some compromised accounts belonged to Fortune 100 companies and US government entities; the initial compromise vector for the accounts has not been established in accessible reporting and the actors are unnamed. UK relevance is specific and acute. This feed has carried, since 11 November, the research finding over 100 serious flaws and leaked credentials across 349 UK public-sector open-source repositories, including the Planning Inspectorate's Entra ID credential left exposed for 18 months. wfx-loot is the industrialised version of exactly that exposure: UK departments, arm's-length bodies, local authorities and their suppliers publish heavily to GitHub under the government's open-source-by-default posture, many use GitHub Actions for deployment, and a growing number federate Azure roles to GitHub OIDC. A single maintainer account compromise in that estate reaches production cloud. Expert commentary carried in this feed on 11 November warned against the reflex of pulling repositories private without remediating first; wfx-loot is the reason that advice matters - going private does not revoke a secret that has already been harvested.
recommended_actions: Search every GitHub organisation you control for open or closed pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes' and for branches named wfx-docs, chore/ followed by 8 characters, or ci-check- followed by 4 characters. These are the campaign's reconnaissance and delivery markers.
Check GitHub Actions workflow run numbering for gaps - Aikido flags missing run numbers as evidence of deleted execution history, which is how the operators covered the stealer's runs.

Treat every GitHub Actions secret and variable in any repository that received an unexpected commit since 10 November 2026 as compromised, and rotate it. Revoking is not enough; assume the value is already held.

Audit GitHub OIDC trust policies in AWS, Azure and GCP now. Constrain the subject claim to specific repositories, branches and environments rather than to the whole organisation, and apply short session durations and minimal role permissions.

Review cloud audit logs (CloudTrail AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, Entra ID federated sign-ins, GCP STS token exchanges) for OIDC-sourced sessions since 10 November 2026 and reconcile each against a known workflow run.

For any account with package-publishing rights to npm, PyPI, Go, crates.io or Packagist, enforce phishing-resistant MFA, rotate publishing tokens, and review recently published versions for unexpected releases.

UK public-sector specifically: resume and complete the secret-scanning and rotation work across the 349 public repositories identified on 11 November. Treat any secret ever committed as compromised, not merely revoked, and do not substitute making repositories private for rotation.
Enable GitHub push protection and secret scanning across all organisations, and require reviewed, signed commits on branches that can trigger workflows with access to secrets.
Pin GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs rather than tags, and restrict which actions may run, so that a compromised upstream action cannot be silently swapped in.

vulnerabilities.title: Apache HTTP Server HTTP/2 Pre-Auth Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-119618, CVSS 9.8) - Carry-Over: Public Reproduction Lab Now Available, Red Hat Confirms Reliable Exploit Against Default Configuration, Still No Confirmed In-the-Wild Exploitation
affected_products: Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 (only where HTTP/2 is enabled)
Standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42
Downstream distribution packages: Debian bookworm/trixie/forky and Amazon Linux reported pending as at 12 November; RHEL 9/10 fixed
Bundled Apache inside vendor appliances, container base images and application stacks
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - cross-cutting, carried over from 12 November with its exploitation picture now clearer and slightly less alarming than the initial reporting implied. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71, released 11 November 2026, fixes CVE-2026-119618, a race condition in mod_http2 that corrupts heap memory and is reported to permit unauthenticated remote code execution at CVSS 9.8. Affected builds are 2.4.55 to 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 2.0.8 to 2.0.42, but only where HTTP/2 is enabled - that is, where the Protocols directive includes h2 or h2c. The in-window development is one of evidence rather than events. Red Hat's advisory states that public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled, and a public reproduction lab is now referenced (googlesky/CVE-2026-119618) alongside the ThreadSanitizer evidence and standard-library HTTP/2 proof-of-concept noted yesterday. Against that, no honeypot telemetry, GreyNoise-style sensor data or incident reporting showing opportunistic scanning or in-the-wild exploitation surfaced in this window, and multiple trackers continue to record no verified exploitation and no KEV listing. The earlier Wiz assessment stating no exploit was available predates the public reproduction material and should be considered superseded. The correct reading is therefore: weaponisable and publicly reproducible, but not yet observed being used. That still argues for urgency, because the distribution patch gap persists - Debian bookworm, trixie and forky and Amazon Linux were reported as having no fixed package, while RHEL 9 and 10 shipped - which means UK organisations patching only from distribution repositories may still have nothing to install, making the configuration workaround the operative control. UK exposure remains disproportionate: Apache fronts a large share of GOV.UK-adjacent services, NHS trust web estates, university and local-authority sites and reverse-proxy tiers in front of Java and PHP applications, and HTTP/2 has been enabled by default in most distribution builds for years. Apache's own advisory lists no workaround; Wiz advises stripping h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving 'Protocols http/1.1'. Detail remains from search-result summaries only.
recommended_actions: If you have not yet done so, inventory every Apache HTTP Server instance and grep the Protocols directive across all vhosts and included config fragments for h2 or h2c. Instances without HTTP/2 are not affected and should be de-prioritised.
Upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 or mod_h2 2.0.43+ wherever a package now exists; re-check the Debian and Amazon Linux security trackers today, as those were the gaps reported yesterday.

Where no package exists yet, apply the mitigation rather than waiting: set 'Protocols http/1.1', remove h2 and h2c, reload, and record the HTTP/2 performance loss as a temporary deviation to revert after patching.
Prioritise internet-facing and DMZ reverse proxies, load-balancer TLS-offload tiers and WAF-origin Apache nodes - these ALPN-negotiate h2 and are reachable pre-authentication.
Check appliance and container images alongside OS packages: bundled Apache inside vendor appliances, Docker base images and application bundles will not be covered by OS patching.
Raise monitoring sensitivity on httpd/apache2 segmentation faults and worker crash-loops; the race condition produces crash noise on failed attempts before successful execution.
Hunt for post-exploitation rather than for the exploit: shells, interpreters and network tooling spawned by the web server account are the reliable signal.
Re-check KEV daily. The combination of a public reproduction lab and a confirmed reliable exploit against a default configuration is the usual precursor to a KEV listing with a short deadline.

vulnerabilities.title: KEV Deadlines Expire TODAY (13 November): Barracuda ESG Pre-Auth Root Chain (CVE-2026-116606 + CVE-2026-111560) and Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 - Last Day for Federal Remediation, Both Under Active Exploitation

Ivanti Connect Secure prior to 25.1.1.3 / 22.8R2.6
Ivanti Policy Secure and ZTA Gateway where the same component is present
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - time-critical carry-over whose deadline is today. Both of these are KEV-listed with a US federal remediation deadline of 13 November 2026, which is the date of this run. UK organisations have no legal obligation to that deadline, but it is the clearest available proxy for 'CISA assesses this is being used against real targets right now', and the NCSC's own guidance treats KEV as a prioritisation input. Barracuda ESG: the chain of CVE-2026-116606 (authentication bypass) and CVE-2026-111560 (root command injection) yields pre-authentication root on an appliance that sits in the mail path and holds message content, directory bind credentials and TLS material. Previdian telemetry carried in this feed on 12 November recorded 17 exploitation attempts from 15 distinct IP addresses across 3 countries between 9 and 11 November - a vendor observation of attempts, not a compromise count, and the attacker addresses were not published. The fixed version is reported as 9.4.0.030, though Barracuda Campus material reportedly says 9.4.0.029 or later; treat 9.4.0.030 as the safe floor. Ivanti Connect Secure: CVE-2026-118527 was exploited as a zero-day alongside CVE-2026-111357 and a third chained flaw, all now KEV-listed. Two cautions carry forward and matter more today than they did yesterday. First, if you patched Ivanti on 13 October you covered only CVE-2026-104935 and remain exposed. Second, Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool may not detect this exploitation because attacker commands execute in memory, so a clean ICT result is not evidence of a clean appliance - any device exposed since 3 October needs credential rotation (LAPS passwords, BitLocker key re-escrow for anything the appliance could reach) rather than a tool-based clearance. Sources continue to disagree on whether CVE-2026-118527 requires a local or a remote authenticated attacker; plan for the worse reading. UK relevance: Ivanti Connect Secure remains widespread across UK central government, NHS trusts, local authorities and legal and financial services as the remote-access tier, and Barracuda ESG is common in UK education, local government and mid-market. Both are edge devices where exploitation is pre- or near-pre-authentication and where compromise is rarely visible from the inside. Note also that the 9 November KEV batch (GPUStack CVE-2026-102895, FreeSWITCH CVE-2026-116779, OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158, IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2026-123218) passed its deadline yesterday - if that work is incomplete it is now overdue, with the OpenSSH 'SSHole' exposure concentrated in Alpine/musl container images and appliance firmware rather than mainstream glibc hosts.
recommended_actions: Today: patch Barracuda ESG to 9.4.0.030 or later and Ivanti Connect Secure to 25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6. If either cannot be patched today, take it off the internet until it can be.
Do not rely on Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool as clearance. Attacker commands run in memory and may leave no on-disk trace; a clean ICT result does not exclude compromise.

For any Ivanti appliance internet-exposed since 3 October 2026, rotate LAPS passwords and re-escrow BitLocker recovery keys for everything the appliance could reach, plus all appliance-resident credentials, certificates and API keys.
If you patched Ivanti on 13 October, re-check: that update addressed CVE-2026-104935 only and leaves CVE-2026-118527 and CVE-2026-111357 unremediated.

For Barracuda ESG, after patching, review mail-flow rules, connectors and forwarding configuration for unauthorised changes, and rotate the appliance's directory bind account and any stored SMTP credentials.
Hunt both appliances for added SSH keys, new local accounts, modified cron entries and unexpected outbound connections, and compare running configuration to a known-good baseline.

Close out the 9 November KEV batch if still open - it is now past deadline. Prioritise OpenSSH CVE-2026-123158 by scanning container registries and appliance firmware for Alpine/musl builds, not just running servers.

vulnerabilities.title: CISA Confirms Active Exploitation of Outlook Zero-Day CVE-2026-124194 (12 November) - NTLMv2 Hash Theft Without the External-Content Warning; Chromium CVE-2026-125350 Also KEV-Listed, Both Due 24 November
affected_products: Microsoft Outlook (desktop) - fixed via the Office update channel, not Windows Update
Microsoft 365 Apps / Office perpetual builds carrying the November 2026 security update
Google Chrome prior to 157.0.8103.50 and Chromium-based browsers (Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - carry-over with a meaningful in-window development. On 12 November CISA was reported to have confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-124194, the Outlook zero-day fixed in Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday and already flagged by Microsoft as 'Exploitation Detected'. Microsoft separately confirmed that attackers are exploiting it to steal Windows authentication hashes. The mechanism is the reason this ranks above its modest CVSS 6.5: an attacker-supplied message file causes Outlook to connect to a remote location without presenting the usual external-content warning, leaking the user's NTLMv2 hash to attacker-controlled infrastructure. There is no payload to detect, no macro to block and no user decision to get wrong - the user sees a message and the hash leaves. Captured NTLMv2 hashes are then cracked offline or relayed, which in a UK public-sector estate with on-premises Active Directory and hybrid Entra ID is a direct path to account takeover. One caution carried forward: one outlet reports that it could not independently verify the exploitation claim against an official CISA advisory, and another notes the reviewed advisory names no attackers, victims, campaign scale or indicators. Treat the confirmation as credible but thinly evidenced. Two operational points remain the practical difference between patched and unpatched. The Outlook fix arrives through the Office update channel, not Windows Update, so an estate that is fully patched at OS level can still be entirely vulnerable - verify Office build numbers specifically. And the compensating control is network-layer: block outbound SMB on TCP/445 and WebDAV at the perimeter so that even a successful trigger cannot reach attacker infrastructure. Consolidated into the same entry is Chromium CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free patched by Google on 9 November and KEV-listed on 10 November with the same 24 November deadline; it is Google's eighth actively exploited zero-day of 2026 and requires a browser relaunch, not merely a downloaded update, to take effect.
recommended_actions: Verify Office build numbers across the estate, not OS patch level. The Outlook fix ships through the Office update channel and an OS-patched device can be fully vulnerable.
Block outbound SMB (TCP/445) and WebDAV at the perimeter for all user subnets. This is the control that neutralises the leak even where patching lags.
Enforce SMB signing and, where feasible, disable NTLM outbound or restrict it to named servers via Group Policy; CVE-2026-124194's value to an attacker is the relayable hash.
Force a Chrome and Edge relaunch to 157.0.8103.50 or later - a downloaded Chromium update does not apply until the browser restarts, and users commonly go weeks without one.
Hunt for outbound SMB and WebDAV attempts from user workstations to public IP addresses over the last 30 days; successful or blocked, these indicate triggered messages.
Review authentication logs for NTLM authentications that do not correspond to expected user activity, particularly from service or privileged accounts.
Prioritise accounts most likely to receive attacker mail - finance, HR, procurement, ministerial private offices and shared mailboxes - for both patch verification and hash-exposure review.
Treat any user whose workstation shows an outbound 445/WebDAV attempt to a public destination as having leaked credentials: reset the password and review subsequent sign-ins.

vulnerabilities.title: 'Fortinet2Shell' (CVE-2026-121529, CVSS 9.1): Drive-By RCE as SYSTEM Against FortiClient Endpoints via Local API Origin-Validation Flaw - Public PoCs Now Available, Most Reliable Where FortiPAM Is Enabled
affected_products: FortiClient for Windows 7.4.0 through 7.4.7 and 7.2.0 through 7.2.14
FortiClient for macOS 7.4.0 through 7.4.7
FortiClient Windows PAM agent 7.4.0 through 7.4.7 and 7.2.0 through 7.2.14
Not affected: FortiClient 8.0
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - endpoint-side exposure that has moved from advisory to armed during this window. Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-194 covers CVE-2026-121529, dubbed 'Fortinet2Shell' by its finder Kevin Joensen of Baldur Security: an origin validation error in a local API endpoint that FortiClient exposes on the loopback interface (reported as 127.0.0.1:9191, service FortiVRS.exe on Windows). Because the endpoint's CORS configuration wrongly trusts cross-origin requests, any web page the user visits while FortiClient is running can send requests to that local service and achieve arbitrary code execution. CVSS is 9.1. What makes this materially worse than a typical client-side bug is the absence of probabilistic steps: the researchers describe it as a deterministic HTTP request with no race window to win, no memory layout to defeat, and no VPN, domain or FortiPAM credentials required. The only prerequisite is that the victim visits a page - the classic watering-hole and malvertising precondition. The in-window change is availability: public proof-of-concept repositories for CVE-2026-121529 have appeared, described as achieving unauthenticated RCE as SYSTEM via the local API. One PoC write-up additionally warns that a CORS-header-only mitigation leaves the attack working in a blind form, meaning partial fixes or WAF-style workarounds are not sufficient and only the fixed releases close it. Fortinet states the flaw is not known to be exploited; with working public exploits and a drive-by trigger, that status should be assumed temporary. UK relevance is broad: FortiClient is one of the most common VPN and endpoint agents across UK central government, local authorities, NHS organisations, further and higher education and the mid-market, and the FortiPAM agent concentrates the risk precisely where privileged-access sessions are brokered - the machines on which SYSTEM-level code execution is worth most. Fixed releases are FortiClient 7.4.8 and 7.2.15; FortiClient 8.0 is unaffected.
recommended_actions: Inventory FortiClient versions across Windows and macOS and upgrade to 7.4.8 or 7.2.15. Prioritise any endpoint with the FortiClient Windows PAM agent, where exploitation is reported to be most reliable.
Do not rely on a CORS-header-only mitigation or a web filter as a substitute for the patch; a PoC write-up reports the attack still succeeds blind against a header-only fix.

Where immediate patching is impossible, check whether the local API service (reported on 127.0.0.1:9191, FortiVRS.exe) can be disabled or firewalled at the host level for your configuration, and confirm with Fortinet support before doing so at scale.
Hunt for local listeners on port 9191 and for FortiVRS.exe spawning child processes - the latter is the post-exploitation signal, since code executes in the service context.

Treat browsers as the delivery path: ensure browser patching is current, enable protections against malicious and newly registered domains, and review web proxy logs for user visits to newly registered or low-reputation domains followed by unusual local process activity.
Prioritise privileged users and administrators for patching first - they are the highest-value targets for a drive-by that yields SYSTEM and are the ones most likely to be running the PAM agent.
Add CVE-2026-121529 to daily KEV monitoring; public PoCs plus a no-credential drive-by trigger is the standard precursor to a KEV listing.
Where FortiClient is deployed on unmanaged or BYOD endpoints used for remote access, consider blocking those devices from connecting until they report a fixed version.

vulnerabilities.title: 'SignDrop' Windows CLFS Zero-Day: Public PoC for Local Privilege Escalation to SYSTEM With No CVE, No Advisory and No Patch - Registry Check Available to Determine Exposure
affected_products: Microsoft Windows - Common Log File System driver (clfs.sys)
Systems where HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication Mode is 0 or 1
Reported secondary involvement of Microsoft Defender's elevated signature-file creation (disputed between sources)
vulnerabilities.summary: UK government and UK corporate - the window's notable unpatched exposure. A researcher operating under the handle Nightmare Eclipse (also reported as MSNightmare and Chaotic Eclipse) published details and a proof-of-concept for 'SignDrop', a local privilege escalation in the Windows Common Log File System that takes a standard user to SYSTEM. There is no CVE, no Microsoft advisory and no patch - nothing addressing it appeared in the November 2026 security updates - so this is an open exposure, not a patching exercise. The technique abuses flawed logic in CLFS authentication: object-manager symbolic links are used to redirect the creation of a CLFS companion file to an attacker-chosen location. Sources differ on the precise mechanism. SecurityWeek describes a standard user coercing Microsoft Defender into creating a signature file with SYSTEM privileges at an attacker-controlled path, while other reports place the defect solely in clfs.sys, the kernel driver implementing CLFS; the researcher's broader claim that the technique generalises to any antimalware engine running with elevated privileges is unverified. Reliability is also contested: the researcher claims it should work on roughly 80 per cent of Windows installations, a figure one report notes has no supporting data, and another researcher found the exploit unreliable for operational use. Cyderes compiled and tested the PoC and found no evidence of in-the-wild exploitation. The practical significance for UK organisations is not that SYSTEM is novel but that CLFS has been one of the most heavily weaponised local privilege escalation surfaces of recent years, repeatedly used as the escalation step in ransomware intrusions; a public, no-CVE, no-patch CLFS technique materially shortens the path from initial foothold to domain-wide impact for any UK department, trust, council or enterprise that suffers a phishing or drive-by compromise. There is a concrete exposure check: read HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication and examine the Mode value, with 0 and 1 reported as the exposed settings. Until Microsoft ships a fix, the defensible posture is detection and containment of the preceding stage rather than prevention of the escalation itself.
recommended_actions: Determine exposure across the estate by reading HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication and recording the Mode value; 0 and 1 are the reported exposed settings. Do this as a reporting exercise first before changing anything.

Do not change the CLFS Authentication Mode value in production without testing. The behaviour of non-default modes is not documented in accessible reporting and could affect logging-dependent applications.

Accept that this cannot currently be patched and invest the effort in the preceding stage: phishing resistance, browser and FortiClient patching (see rank 7), application control and removal of local administrator rights, so that an attacker never reaches the point of needing escalation.

Tune EDR for CLFS-specific behaviour: .blf and container file creation in unusual paths, object-manager symbolic link creation by non-system processes, and unexpected writes to Defender signature directories.

Alert on a standard user process whose child or subsequent activity runs as SYSTEM without a known service or scheduled-task origin - the generic escalation signal that catches this and its successors.
Monitor for a Microsoft advisory and CVE assignment daily; given a public PoC, assignment and a patch are likely, and the KEV listing could follow quickly if exploitation begins.
Verify Microsoft Defender tamper protection is enabled and that signature paths are monitored, given the disputed reporting that Defender's elevated file creation is part of the chain.
Treat any host where this technique succeeds as fully compromised: SYSTEM allows credential material extraction, so plan for credential rotation rather than host cleanup.

kql.name: CLFS Authentication Mode inventory (SignDrop exposure check)
kql.description: Untested. Surfaces the exposure-determining registry value across the estate. Reported exposed values are Mode 0 and Mode 1.
kql.query:
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where RegistryKey has "CurrentControlSet\\Services\\CLFS\\Authentication"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "Mode"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, RegistryValueData) by DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName
| extend Exposure = case(RegistryValueData in ("0", "1", "0x0", "0x1"), "EXPOSED", "review")
| project DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, Exposure, Timestamp
| order by Exposure asc, DeviceName asc

kql.name: CLFS container / .blf file creation in unusual locations
kql.description: Untested. SignDrop redirects creation of a CLFS companion file to an attacker-chosen path. Legitimate CLFS files live in well-known system locations; creations elsewhere by user-context processes are the signal.
kql.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where FileName endswith ".blf" or FileName has "CLFS" or FolderPath has "BLF"
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\Windows\\System32\\config", "\\Windows\\System32\\LogFiles", "\\Windows\\ServiceProfiles", "\\System Volume Information"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Unexpected writes to Microsoft Defender signature paths
kql.description: Untested. Addresses the disputed variant in which Defender is coerced into creating a file with SYSTEM privileges at an attacker-chosen location. Writes to Defender paths by anything other than Defender itself warrant review.
kql.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\Windows Defender\\Definition Updates", "\\Windows Defender\\Scans", "\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender", "\\ProgramData\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "MpSigStub.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "svchost.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Standard user context escalating to SYSTEM without a service origin
kql.description: Untested. Technique-agnostic escalation detection. This will fire on legitimate elevation paths, so baseline installers, scheduled tasks and service controllers before alerting.
kql.query:
let KnownElevators = dynamic(["services.exe", "svchost.exe", "taskhostw.exe", "wininit.exe", "msiexec.exe", "TiWorker.exe", "TrustedInstaller.exe", "consent.exe", "MsMpEng.exe"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(21d)
| where AccountName in~ ("system", "nt authority\\system")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system", "nt authority\\system", "local service", "network service")
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) !in (KnownElevators)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.summary: UK corporate - the window's UK victim picture, and it should be read with its confidence rating in mind. Two new UK listings appeared on extortion leak sites during the window: bristol-companies.com, claimed by the Settra group and recorded by ransomware.live at 19:10 UTC on 12 November with an estimated attack date of 16 October 2026, and sdcc.net, also listed as a GB victim on 12 November but with no further detail located. The month-long gap between the estimated attack date and the listing for bristol-companies is the familiar extortion rhythm - negotiation first, publication when it fails - and it means the intrusion itself sits well outside this window. Carrying over from the previous two days: Audio Note UK Ltd, listed by Osiris on 11 November with an estimated attack date of 26 October; A&O Shearman, the UK-headquartered international law firm, appearing in breach-tracking listings with a discovery date of 10-11 November and no clear ransomware characterisation; and Signworx, listed by Play on 10 November. The one item with an actual company statement remains Maersk, which confirmed on 11-12 November the theft of data from a legacy system inherited through its LF Logistics acquisition, with the group WhiteArmor demanding USD 5 million in bitcoin - the same group that listed UK-headquartered Unilever on 5 November. Every assertion here other than Maersk's own confirmation is an unverified criminal claim. No victim statements, ICO notifications or press confirmations were located for any of the UK listings, N0N-family listings have previously been reported to include fabricated victims, and the trackers themselves are aggregators rather than authoritative sources. The value of the entry is pattern rather than fact: the UK mid-market and professional-services sector continues to absorb a steady stream of extortion listings from a widening set of smaller brands - Settra, Osiris, Play, WhiteArmor, Hyflock, Vexy - with no single dominant group, and the Maersk case illustrates the specific and recurring failure mode of acquired legacy systems that never entered the parent's security programme. That is the transferable lesson for UK acquirers: due diligence that stops at the closing date leaves an unmonitored estate carrying the parent's brand and the parent's regulatory exposure.
recommended_actions: If your organisation, a subsidiary or a named supplier appears in these listings, treat it as a live incident until disproved: preserve logs immediately, engage incident response, and assess ICO notification obligations against the 72-hour clock from awareness.

Monitor extortion leak sites for your own brands, trading names, acquired entities and key suppliers daily rather than relying on being told - all but one of these victims learned of it from the listing.

Audit acquired and legacy systems specifically. The Maersk case is a legacy system inherited through acquisition; run a discovery exercise for estates that never completed onboarding into monitoring, patching and identity governance.

Map your professional-services supply chain - legal, accountancy, payroll, recruitment - and confirm each firm's breach-notification commitments. The A&O Shearman listing is a reminder that privileged client data concentrates in these firms.

For UK mid-market organisations without 24/7 monitoring, prioritise the basics these groups rely on: MFA on all remote access, no internet-exposed RDP, offline or immutable backups with a tested restore, and EDR on servers as well as workstations.
Rehearse the extortion decision before you face it: who authorises contact, who speaks publicly, what your position on payment is, and what your ICO and law-enforcement reporting path looks like.
Report incidents to the NCSC and Action Fraud; the NCSC Annual Review's incident figures depend on reporting and under-reporting degrades the national picture that UK defenders rely on.
Do not act on an unverified leak-site listing as though it were confirmed when communicating externally - verify first, then communicate, to avoid amplifying a fabricated claim.

vulnerabilities.title: UK Government Window Status: Cyber Security and Resilience Bill Returns to the Commons With Managed Service Providers Now Explicitly In Scope as 'Relevant MSPs'; Gibraltar Incident Still Unresolved; No New UK Government Cyber Incident Confirmed In-Window
vulnerabilities.vendor: UK Government / DSIT / Information Commissioner's Office / NCSC
affected_products: UK operators of essential services and digital service providers under the NIS Regulations 2018 regime
Medium and large managed service providers newly in scope as Relevant Managed Service Providers (RMSPs), regulated by the Information Commission

vulnerabilities.summary: UK government - this entry exists to state plainly what the window did and did not contain. No new UK government cyber incident first reported between 12 and 13 November 2026 was confirmed by this collection. Searches against UK government, NCSC, departmental and sector sources surfaced only items already carried in this feed or dated outside the window, and no NCSC advisory dated 12 or 13 November was located. What did move is regulatory, and it matters because of what sits at rank 1 of this very report. The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill completed its Lords stages with third reading on 2 November 2026 and has returned to the Commons for consideration of Lords amendments. Four government amendments were agreed, including one clarifying that a 'regulated person' covers managed service providers: medium and large MSPs enter the UK NIS regime for the first time as Relevant Managed Service Providers, regulated by the Information Commission, with their own security duties and incident-reporting obligations. Smaller providers appear to fall outside that scope. Ministers have separately indicated an intention to bring some smaller cloud providers into a national security mechanism alongside larger firms. The ConnectWise ScreenConnect compromise of 11-12 November is, in effect, the policy case study arriving ahead of the policy: a third-party extension flaw in an MSP tool reached 288 endpoints across 48 downstream organisations inside 90 minutes, and under the Bill as amended, MSPs of that kind would owe reporting duties for exactly such an event. UK public-sector bodies should not wait for commencement - the contractual lever exists now, and rank 1 contains the questions to ask. Two carry-overs remain open with no in-window development. The HM Government of Gibraltar cloud compromise, flagged to the territory by Microsoft and supported by NCSC specialists who travelled on 2 November, is described by the Government as contained but still under forensic investigation, with whether information was accessed or extracted explicitly unresolved and no attribution; the latest official position located remains that of around 9 November. The NCSC's Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme for CNI operators, launched 12 November at MVP stage, remains current for procurement planning, as does the Annual Review's assessment of 1,831 reported attacks in the year to 31 August 2026, 80 nationally significant incidents, an estimated GBP 14.7 billion annual cost, and the judgement that AI-enabled ransomware against UK CNI is highly likely by 2028.
recommended_actions: Public-sector and CNI bodies: inventory your managed service providers now and classify them against the Bill's likely RMSP threshold, so that contractual security and notification clauses are in place before commencement rather than after.

Insert or strengthen incident-notification clauses in MSP and IT-outsourcing contracts with a defined timescale, a named contact and an obligation to disclose compromise of the provider's own management tooling - not merely of your data.

Use the ScreenConnect event at rank 1 as a live supplier-assurance exercise today: ask each provider what remote-management tooling they use, whether it is cloud-hosted, what third-party extensions are installed and how they would notify you of a console compromise.
MSPs reading this: begin preparing for RMSP obligations now - security measures, incident reporting to the Information Commission, and the evidence base to demonstrate both.

CNI operators and their regulators: engage with the NCSC CyAS scheme at MVP stage, but note the assumed-breach methodology is recommended only for organisations with mature detection capability. If yours is not, invest in telemetry and detection engineering first.

Organisations with operations, suppliers or staff connected to Gibraltar government services: continue to treat the incident as unresolved, maintain heightened vigilance for phishing referencing government correspondence, and do not assume absence of data theft.

Benchmark against the NCSC Annual Review's finding that public-facing application exploits, phishing, misuse of valid accounts and external remote service exploitation account for 88 per cent of incidents at large organisations - and check your controls cover all four, not three.
Report incidents to the NCSC: the national picture that informs this feed and government policy depends on reporting volume, and under-reporting degrades it.

summary_statistics.highest_priority_action: Four things today, in this order. (1) ASK YOUR MSP, TODAY: establish in writing whether any provider with remote access to your estate runs ConnectWise ScreenConnect, whether it is cloud-hosted and whether any 'RMM+' family extension was installed. Attackers took over cloud ScreenConnect consoles and pushed the SCKit toolkit to 288 endpoints across 48 organisations in a 90-minute burst from approximately 17:47 UTC on 11 November. Disable RMM+ extensions in on-premises deployments yourself - ConnectWise has only disabled them in cloud environments - hunt for second unauthorised ScreenConnect clients and for Defender exclusions added in the last week, and do NOT triage suspected infections by connecting through ScreenConnect, because the responder's own machine is at risk. (2) TWO KEV DEADLINES EXPIRE TODAY: Barracuda ESG CVE-2026-116606 + CVE-2026-111560 (patch to 9.4.0.030 or later) and Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2026-118527 (patch to 25.1.1.3 or 22.8R2.6). If you patched Ivanti on 13 October you covered only CVE-2026-104935 and remain exposed, and the Integrity Checker Tool may return clean on a compromised appliance because attacker commands run in memory - rotate LAPS passwords and re-escrow BitLocker keys for anything reachable from an appliance exposed since 3 October. The 9 November batch (GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH 'SSHole', IBM Aspera Faspex) was due yesterday and is now overdue. (3) CHECK POINT GATEWAYS AND THE PATH TO YOUR HYPERVISORS: patch Mobile Access gateways against PHP2Shell and CVE-2026-123039, then treat patching as insufficient - any portal exposed and unpatched since mid-October needs a compromise assessment. The campaign ends in a wiper on ESXi, not encryption, so block gateway-to-ESXi SSH, enable lockdown mode, and verify that virtualisation backups are offline or immutable and that a restore has actually been tested. (4) GITHUB AND CI CREDENTIALS: search every organisation you control for pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes' and branches named wfx-docs, chore/{8} or ci-check-{4}, look for gaps in Actions workflow run numbering, rotate every Actions secret in any repository touched since 10 November, and constrain GitHub OIDC trust policies to specific repositories and branches - the stealer exchanges OIDC tokens for live AWS, Azure and GCP sessions, so a repository compromise is a cloud compromise. UK public-sector bodies should resume the secret-scanning work across the 349 public repositories identified on 11 November and treat every secret ever committed as compromised, not merely revoked. In parallel: upgrade FortiClient to 7.4.8 or 7.2.15 (public PoCs now exist for a drive-by RCE as SYSTEM, worst where FortiPAM is enabled); verify Office build numbers rather than OS patch level for the Outlook zero-day and block outbound SMB/445 and WebDAV; force a Chrome relaunch to 157.0.8103.50+; set 'Protocols http/1.1' on any Apache instance with h2 enabled that has no fixed package yet; and inventory the CLFS Authentication Mode registry value to scope SignDrop exposure, which has no patch available.
